Both laser cooling and optical trapping have revolutionized atomic physics, enabling 
unprecedented control over atomic and nanoparticle degrees of freedom. They serve as a
crucial gateway, offering insights into fundamental physics and opening the way for diverse
quantum technologies. These technologies are used in various applications, ranging from 
atomic sensors to quantum computers [8], quantum simulators [9], and atomic clocks [10].
Molecular structure dictates that optical cycling must operate on a Type-II transition (F′ = F−1
or F′ = F) for rotational closure. To date, several molecular species have been laser cooled and

trapped in a MOT [11]. Among these molecules, CaF, SrF, YO, CaOH, and SrOH have been 
further cooled to ultracold temperatures (∼5−100μK) and loaded into conservative Optical 
Dipole Traps (ODTs) [12]. These developments indicate that Type-II transitions are well-suited 
for use in various quantum science applications. While atomic laser cooling (Doppler and 
Sisyphus mechanisms) led to the development of exceptional atomic clocks and atom 
interferometers, atomic systems suffer from low absolute mass, limiting their coupling to
gravitational forces or subtle macroscopic accelerations.

This research proposal outlines a comprehensive work to investigate, model, and 
experimentally realize the non-equilibrium quantum dynamics of levitated dielectric 
nanoparticles within optical traps under UHV regimes. Levitated optomechanics offers a 
unique paradigm for precision sensing, as the physical isolation of a macroscopic object from 
a physical substrate removes structural clamping losses, yielding mechanical quality factors 
exceeding Q > 10^9. 
This proposal also investigates the fundamental and non-linear trap dynamics - including 
Doppler limits, sub-Doppler Sisyphus cooling, optical lattice potentials, and real-time 
parametric feedback - to suppress thermal noise and enhance the sensitivity of next-generation 
inertial and gravitational sensors. Also the use of laser-cooled Group IV atoms for precision 
measurements and tests of fundamental physics, including atomic parity violation will be 
explored. 
7. Expected Outcomes and Deliverables 
1. A comprehensive theoretical and numerical model of multi-stage cooling dynamics for 
atomic species (e.g., Alkali, Group-IV, or alkaline-earth analogs). 
2. Experimental demonstration of an enhanced phase-space density configuration tailored 
for compact quantum sensors and tests of fundamental physics, including atomic parity 
variation. 
3. A validated, high-performance software package implementing the Lindblad Master 
Equation and QJMC solvers for gray molasses and lattice-loading optimization, to be 
made available for the wider atomic, molecular, and optical (AMO) physics 
community. 
4. A comprehensive data-driven map correlating magnetic field ramp-down rates, laser 
detuning trajectories, and lattice depths with final phase-space densities across diverse 
atomic species.

8. Organization of the Thesis  
The organization of the thesis is outlined as follows: 
Chapter 1, titled “Introduction,” introduces the importance of laser cooling and trapping of 
atoms in MOT. It highlights the challenges of sub-Doppler cooling techniques. It outlines the 
motivation and structure of the thesis, providing a foundation for further exploration. 
Chapter 2, titled “Literature Review,” critically evaluates existing research, builds the 
theoretical and conceptual frameworks, and explicitly identifies the research gap. 
Chapter 3, titled “Theoretical Framework,” explores the physics of light-atom interactions. It 
discusses the mathematical formulation of laser cooling and trapping for different atomic 
systems. 
Chapter 4, titled “Experimental Details,” offers a concise overview of the tools and techniques 
utilized in the following chapters. It covers the atomic structure of the element used, the laser 
system, spectroscopy and characterization techniques, and an outline of the computer control 
system. 
Chapter 5, titled “Results,” presents the factual findings, interprets what the results mean and 
compares them with prior literature reviewed in Chapter 2. 
Chapter 6, titled “Conclusions and Future Work,” highlights successes in laser cooling and 
trapping. It also summarizes key findings from spectroscopy and experimental 
characterization. Further, promising directions for future research are also outlined.
